W.E.B. Du Bois. An intellectual giant of the twentieth century—a sociologist, historian, civil rights activist, and founding member of the NAACP whose concept of double consciousness defined the African-American experience. His prolific writing and organizing work made him a towering presence in Black thought and activism from the early nineteen-hundreds until his death in Ghana in 1963. In 1905 he founded the Niagara Movement, the first major Black-led civil rights organization, challenging Booker T. Washington's accommodationist approach. Four years later, in 1909, he helped found the NAACP and served as editor of its magazine The Crisis for twenty-four years, using it to reach and mobilize the Black community. In 1903 he wrote The Souls of Black Folk, a seminal collection of essays introducing the concept of double consciousness—the Black American's dual identity as both Black and American. He coined the term the Talented Tenth to describe the educated Black elite he believed would lead racial advancement. He spent decades as a sociology professor and produced groundbreaking empirical work on Black communities, institutions, and social conditions. Over his lifetime he moved to the political left, becoming increasingly critical of capitalism and aligned with socialist thought in his later years. In 1961 at age ninety-three he emigrated to Ghana, rejecting American racism, and died there two years later. He was the ideological opponent of Booker T. Washington, disagreeing fundamentally on strategy for Black advancement—accommodation versus agitation. He was skeptical of Marcus Garvey, his competitor for influence over the movement. Yet intellectually he was a predecessor to Malcolm X's pan-African and separatist thinking. And he was an intellectual predecessor whose institutional civil rights legacy the NAACP carried forward, with Martin Luther King Jr. becoming the inheritor of that legacy.
